e.t: This Greek LXX noun means “purchase”—something bought or the act of acquiring something by payment. It refers broadly to buying rather than to a particular kind of object or transaction. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including passages from Genesis, Nehemiah, Proverbs, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Azēr, also rendered Azir, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 4:4. Because names identify people, its basic meaning is the individual named Azēr; the surrounding genealogy is needed to understand his family connection and significance in that passage. The name itself does not provide a broader definition or theme beyond identifying this person.

This adjective means “unceasing”: something that does not stop or come to an end. It describes continuing action, activity, or condition rather than something brief or interrupted. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:2. The word’s exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains continuous persistence. It is therefore a term for what keeps going without cessation.

This Greek LXX verb means to pay no regard to something or someone—to disregard it rather than give it attention or weight. It describes an action, not a person or object, so its sense centers on refusing to take something into account. In the LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 12:24. The precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text, but the word’s basic idea remains clear: treating something as unworthy of notice or consideration.

Amri is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 9:4. Because the available text does not provide the surrounding verse, this entry identifies the name itself but does not assign further significance or describe the person beyond that occurrence. The name is rendered consistently as “Amri,” preserving it as a proper name rather than translating it as an ordinary descriptive word.

“Murder” is a verb describing the deliberate killing of a person. It expresses human violence resulting in death, rather than merely referring to danger, injury, or ordinary death. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, this word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 9:15. Its lexical meaning is direct and specific, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain how the word functions in that particular sentence.

This noun means “lawlessness”: conduct or a condition that rejects or disregards what the law requires. It describes behavior viewed as outside the proper bounds of law, rather than simply an ordinary mistake. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, it occurs 209 times, showing that the term is used broadly in descriptions of wrongdoing and moral disorder. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “tender,” describing something soft, delicate, or not hardened. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for people or things characterized by gentleness or delicacy rather than strength or toughness. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, including passages in Genesis, Deuteronomy, Chronicles, Isaiah, and Wisdom. Its exact force in any verse depends on what person or thing it describes there.

This Greek LXX noun means “spreading out.” It describes the act or result of something extending outward rather than remaining gathered in one place. As a noun, it names that outward extension. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, at Job 36:29. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here; its basic sense remains outward extension.

This verb means “run away,” describing a person leaving or escaping from a place or situation. It presents departure as a decisive act of getting away, rather than simply remaining absent. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs 29 times, showing repeated use for flight or escape across different passages. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains running away.

This word means that someone has lost all sense—they are no longer thinking clearly or acting with sound judgment. As a verb, it describes a state of mental confusion or irrational conduct rather than a deliberate decision. It appears once in the Greek LXX, at 2 Maccabees.13.23, though the surrounding verse text is not available here. The surrounding context determines how that loss of sense is expressed there.

This Greek LXX verb means “deflower” or “violate,” describing the act of taking a woman’s virginity, especially in a forcibly harmful or dishonoring way. Its wording points to an action against a person rather than a general feeling or condition. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 20:4. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains an act of defilement or violation.

This verb means to “thrust away” or “reject”—to refuse something or drive it off rather than receive or retain it. It is used 68 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek books represented in this corpus, describing an act of repudiation or removal. The English rendering “reject” appears in some passages, fitting the central sense. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what person or thing is being refused.

This Greek LXX verb means “enough” or “content”: it expresses that something is sufficient or that a person is satisfied with what is available. It can describe having an adequate amount, or being satisfied rather than needing more. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so its basic sense appears across several kinds of passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

Arsōn is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship, so its meaning is primarily the individual’s name. This name occurs three times in the Greek text, all within 1 Chronicles: 1 Chronicles 2:5, 4:1, and 5:3. The available lexical information gives the name as “Arsōn,” also represented as “Arson.”

Astaōl is a proper name rendered as “Astaol,” rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 15:33, so its meaning is chiefly the identification of the named entity to which the passage refers. The name itself does not carry an ordinary descriptive meaning such as a virtue, emotion, or command. Its precise referent is determined by the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “lead from”: it describes directing or bringing someone away from a starting place, position, or group. As a verb, it expresses an action performed by someone who guides another person or people from one point to another. It occurs 31 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages from Exodus, Judges, and Ezekiel, and also in several deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

Balad, also rendered Valath, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a specific named individual or place, but the available wording does not establish which. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 1 Chronicles 7:29. Its exact reference there should be understood from the surrounding verse and passage rather than from the name alone. The two forms, Balad and Valath, are the approved English renderings of this single proper name.

This word means “queen,” referring to a woman who holds royal rank or serves as the female ruler or royal consort in the Old Testament Greek Scriptures. It is a noun used for queens in royal settings, including accounts associated with Solomon, Esther, and other kingdoms. The word occurs 39 times in the Greek Old Testament, showing a recurring term for women connected with kingship and palace authority. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains a queen.

Boasom, also rendered Voasom, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available information does not establish which kind of name it is. This name occurs once in the Greek text, at 1 Chronicles 4:29. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and genealogy, which are not included here.

Gargasi is a proper name rendered as “Gargasi.” It identifies a specific person, place, or group rather than expressing a general quality or action; the word information does not establish which kind of named entity it is. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 3:14. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from that verse and its surrounding passage, not from the name alone.

This Greek LXX verb means “laugh”: to express amusement, joy, disbelief, or scorn through laughter, depending on the surrounding sentence. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, including several occurrences in Genesis and Job. Its precise emotional force is determined by the passage in which someone laughs, but its central meaning remains the act of laughing.

This word means “farmer,” a person who works the land and grows or tends crops. It is a noun naming someone engaged in agricultural work, rather than describing the land itself or the work as an activity. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs nine times, with uses spread across Genesis, Jeremiah, Amos, Joel, and Wisdom. Its central meaning remains straightforward: a farmer is a person responsible for cultivating land and producing its yield.

This noun refers to a weak woman. It describes a female person whose condition is marked by weakness, rather than simply identifying any woman. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 24:21. The passage reference identifies where the word appears, but the word’s basic meaning remains “weak woman”; its fuller force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. This word is distinct to the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here.

This verb means “worry”: it expresses troubled concern or anxious care rather than naming a person or object. As a verb, it describes what someone does when inwardly troubled. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs once, at 1 Samuel.10.2. That single occurrence does not by itself define the surrounding situation; the word gives the basic sense, while the passage supplies its particular force.

This word means “jail,” a place where people are confined or held in custody. It is a noun naming the place itself, rather than the act of imprisoning someone or the person held there. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across seven verses, from Genesis through Isaiah. Its uses include settings associated with imprisonment, but the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “carry over”: to move a person or thing from one side or place to another. It describes an action of transferring or bringing across, rather than merely remaining in place. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Genesis, Numbers, Joshua, and 2 Samuel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being carried and where it is brought.

This Greek LXX verb means “slip through”: to pass through or get past something, likely describing movement that avoids being stopped. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Samuel 17:49. Because the word appears only there and the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage. Its central idea remains movement through or past an obstacle.

This noun means “distinction”: a difference that separates one thing, person, or category from another. It names the act or result of recognizing that something is not the same as something else. In the LXX corpus, it occurs four times, appearing in Exodus, Numbers, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a clear separation or difference between things being considered.

This verb means to “burn through,” describing fire moving through something. In the Greek Old Testament text represented here, it appears only once, at Psalm 82:15, so its broader range cannot be established from repeated examples. It is an action word: it presents burning as something that passes through material rather than merely naming fire itself. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording.

gl: plea in justification; speech in defence of sb
d: plea in justification; speech in defence of sb

e.t: This noun refers to a plea offered in justification or a speech made in defence of someone. It describes a spoken argument intended to support a person’s case or provide a defence. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:44. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning is a verbal defence or plea on another’s behalf.

This adjective describes someone or something ungodly or impious—lacking proper reverence toward God and showing disregard for what is holy. It functions as a descriptive word rather than naming a person, place, or action by itself. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs seven times, all in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. The wording can describe people or conduct marked by irreverence, but the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means to mock at—to treat someone or something with scorn or ridicule. It describes an act of derisive speech or behavior rather than a neutral observation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in the book of Job. The word’s precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains an expression of contempt directed toward another. Its two occurrences are Job 40:19 and Job 41:25.

This verb means “pour in”: it describes putting a liquid into something by pouring it. As an action word, it focuses on the movement of the liquid into its destination, rather than merely on the liquid itself. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs three times, in Exodus 24:6, 2 Kings 4:41, and Jeremiah 31:11. The surrounding verse determines what is being poured and into what.

This verb means “accustom”: to make someone familiar with something through repeated practice or regular exposure. It can describe forming a settled habit or becoming used to a particular way of acting. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, in Sirach and 2 Maccabees, so its basic sense is consistent but its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence. It expresses an action of habituating rather than a single, isolated encounter.

This verb means “hang out” or “hang upon,” describing something that remains suspended or clings closely. It expresses the act of hanging rather than naming an object or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 44:30. Because it appears only there and no verse text is provided here, its exact force in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the idea of hanging or depending closely upon something.

This word means “oil,” a substance obtained from olives and used in ordinary life and worship. It is a noun naming the material itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 192 times, showing that oil is a regularly mentioned part of biblical life rather than a rare term. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on how the surrounding text uses it.

This word means “me,” referring to the speaker or person being identified in a sentence. It is a pronoun, so it points to a person rather than naming that person directly. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 232 times, showing regular use in speech, prayer, statements, and descriptions involving the speaker or another person as the object of attention. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something that hinders, obstructs, or gets in the way. It refers to a quality or action that makes progress more difficult rather than helping it move forward. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX text, both within one verse of 4 Maccabees, so its established sense is clear even though the available record does not include the verse text. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “work out” or “make completely.” It describes carrying something through to its finished result rather than merely beginning or attempting it. As a verb, it points to accomplishment, with the surrounding sentence determining what is being brought to completion. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament portion represented here, in Esther and Psalms. The basic idea is purposeful completion: something is fully carried out or made complete.

This adjective describes someone or something worthy of praise—“praiseworthy” or “laudable.” It identifies a quality that merits approval or commendation rather than merely attracting attention. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Ezekiel 26:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains clear: the person or thing described is deserving of favorable recognition.

gl: stepping upon; approaching: a means of approach
d: stepping upon; approaching: a means of approach

e.t: This noun means “stepping upon; approaching” and can refer to “a means of approach.” It describes movement toward or onto something, or the way access is gained. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, including passages in Psalms, Wisdom, and Song of Songs. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains an approach or means of reaching something.

This Greek LXX noun means “slaughter,” referring to the killing of people, usually as an act of destruction rather than an individual death. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament portion represented here, at Deuteronomy 28:25. The word itself names the destructive killing, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how that slaughter is presented and what it signifies in context. Its central sense remains straightforward: a violent mass killing or devastating defeat involving many people.

This Greek LXX verb means “load”: it describes placing something onto something or someone. As a verb, it names the action rather than the thing being loaded. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 13 times across 12 verses, from Genesis through Jeremiah, showing a recurring practical action in biblical narratives. The exact object and force of the word in any particular verse must be understood from that verse’s surrounding text.

This noun means “good arrangement” or “good condition”: a state in which things are properly ordered, organized, or in sound shape. It can describe orderly arrangement rather than a specific object or action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. The precise shade depends on what is being described in the sentence, but the central idea remains orderliness or favorable condition.

This word is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament, rendered as “Ēlōnmaōnenim; Ilonmaonenim.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at Judges 9:37. The available information does not provide a translatable common meaning for the name, so it should be understood primarily as a proper designation.

This verb means “silently” or “still silent,” describing someone who remains quiet rather than speaking. It presents silence as an ongoing action or condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezra 9:3–4. Without the surrounding verse text, the word itself establishes the person’s quietness but does not specify whether that silence reflects sorrow, restraint, attention, or another circumstance.

This word means “death”—the end of a person’s earthly life. It is a noun that names death as a real condition or event, including the sentence or consequence of dying. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 332 times across 319 verses, showing that it is used broadly in discussions of human life, judgment, danger, and mortality. Its central meaning remains straightforward: the passing from life into death. The exact force in a particular verse depends on its surrounding context.

Thekemina is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. It appears once in the Greek LXX, at 1 Kings 11:20. Because the available biblical wording does not provide a definition or description of the person beyond this name, its specific significance cannot be stated from the name alone. The word’s normal function is simply to designate Thekemina as an individual in that passage.

This noun means “shift.” It names a thing, not the action of changing position or taking another person’s place. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs six times, in six verses across Genesis, 1 Samuel, Isaiah, and Song of Songs. Because the word identifies an object by name, its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the wording and surrounding context there.

Idaer is a proper name—the personal name represented by “Idaer” or “Ithaer.” It appears once in the Greek Septuagint, in 1 Chronicles 6:12. Because the available information identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, it does not establish anything further about Idaer’s identity, role, or significance. Its basic meaning is therefore a person’s name, while its precise significance depends on the passage in which it occurs.

Iemna is a personal name, rendered as “Iemna.” It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament translation corpus, the name occurs three times, in Genesis 46:17, 1 Chronicles 7:30, and 2 Chronicles 31:14. The available lexical information identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse text is needed to explain which person is meant in each occurrence and how that person functions in the passage.

Iermias is a personal name, referring to someone identified by that name. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 12:5. Because it is a proper name rather than a common noun or action word, its meaning is chiefly identification: it distinguishes one person from others in the passage. The name itself does not describe a general quality, command, event, or spiritual principle; its role is to name the individual called Iermias.

This noun means “learning by inquiry” or “inquiry”—the pursuit of understanding through careful investigation and questioning. It can describe the process of seeking knowledge rather than a single piece of information. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including passages in Esther, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on how the surrounding sentence presents the act of investigating or learning.

This Greek LXX verb means “sit down” or “seat.” It describes taking a seated position, or causing someone else to sit. Thus, its basic sense can refer either to a person sitting or to someone seating another person, depending on the sentence. It occurs 207 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, so it is a regularly used word for physical positioning rather than a rare or specialized expression.

This word means “fruitful”: producing fruit, results, or a rich yield. As an adjective, it describes something marked by abundance and productive life rather than barrenness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, including passages in Psalms and Hosea, and it is rendered “fruitful” in both occurrences. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is clear: yielding beneficial increase or being richly productive.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “sink down” or “drown.” It describes going beneath the surface or being overwhelmed in water, and it can also portray something or someone being brought down into the depths. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages from Exodus, 2 Samuel, Psalms, Ecclesiastes, and Lamentations. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains sinking beneath or causing something to go under.

This Greek LXX verb expresses becoming little or small. It describes reduction in size or extent rather than greatness or enlargement. Its stated meaning is “little; small,” and its English rendering is “little.” The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament translation, in 2 Samuel 7:19, so its normal lexical sense is clear even though its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. This is a verb, indicating an action or state involving becoming small.

Kitieis, also rendered Kitis, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is therefore tied to the named person, people, or place identified by the surrounding passage, which is not included here. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, it occurs twice: once in Isaiah 23:12 and once in 1 Maccabees 8:5. The spelling and reference distinguish it as a specific name within these passages.

This word means “any dangerous animal,” referring to a creature that poses a serious threat. It is a noun used to name such an animal rather than to describe an action or quality. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in the book of Wisdom. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “acquire”: to obtain or come to possess something. It describes gaining property, possessions, or other things that can become one’s own. The word occurs 97 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, so its central idea is broad but consistent: receiving or securing something for possession. The surrounding passage determines what is acquired and how the action should be understood in a particular verse.

This proper noun names the people called “Lakaidaimonioi” or “Lakethemoni.” It is a group name rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:9. Because the available wording preserves the name in transliterated form and no verse text is provided here, its clearest meaning is the designation of that people. Its precise role in the verse depends on the surrounding context.

Leuïs, also written Leis, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person in the Greek LXX corpus and appears once, in 4 Maccabees 2:19. The name itself does not provide enough information to explain the person’s identity, role, or significance; those details would require the surrounding verse and passage. Thus, its basic meaning is simply the proper name Leuïs or Leis.

This noun means “account.” It refers to an account as something that can be considered, stated, or kept track of, rather than describing an action or a person. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 112 times, so it is a recurring term rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any passage depends on how the surrounding sentence uses the account.

This noun refers to abuse or reproach—language or treatment that expresses insult, blame, or dishonor. Its central idea is a hostile or demeaning response directed toward someone. The word appears once in the LXX corpus, at Exodus 17:7. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its exact force in that occurrence must be understood from the immediate context. Its basic meaning remains a reproachful or abusive act or expression.

Magōg is a proper name rendered “Magog.” It identifies a named figure or people in the Old Testament Greek, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament: in Genesis 10:2, 1 Chronicles 1:5, and Ezekiel 38:2. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic lexical function is to name Magog.

This Greek LXX verb means “softened”: it describes becoming less firm, hardened, or resistant. As a verb, it expresses a change taking place rather than simply naming a quality. It occurs eight times across seven Old Testament verses in the Greek LXX, from Genesis through Isaiah. The word appears in passages involving different people and situations, so its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording and context.

This noun means an “armlet,” a band or ornament worn around the arm. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Daniel chapter 5. The word identifies a personal item rather than an action, quality, or title. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a wearable arm ornament.

Machnadabou is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It is also rendered as Makhnathavu. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Ezra 10:40. Because no broader usage or verse text is available here, the name itself does not provide a further general meaning. Its identification is therefore limited to this personal name and its single occurrence in Ezra.

This noun means “black cummin,” naming a particular plant or seasoning. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Isaiah 28:25 and Isaiah 28:27. The word therefore identifies a specific agricultural item rather than expressing an action, quality, or relationship. Its precise role in each verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the name of black cummin. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus.

This noun means “turning from,” describing a movement away from something or someone. It presents the idea of a reversal or departure rather than remaining on the former course. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in 1 Kings and once in 2 Chronicles, so its precise emphasis depends on the surrounding sentence. The word itself focuses on the act or change of turning away, not merely a physical direction.

This adjective means “solitary,” describing someone or something that stands alone or is separate from others. It expresses singleness or isolation rather than a group or gathered company. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 79:14. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains clear: being alone or apart.

This noun means “scorn” or “contempt”—an attitude that treats someone with disrespect or considers them beneath regard. It names an expression of disdain rather than admiration or honor. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including passages from Nehemiah, Job, Psalms, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Naphlazōn, also rendered Naflazon, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament and occurs once, in Joshua 15:62. Since the available information does not specify whether the name refers to a person, settlement, or another place or entity, its safest meaning is simply the name Naphlazōn or Naflazon. Its exact significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun refers to a legislator—a person associated with making or establishing laws. It identifies the one who gives law, rather than the law itself. In the Greek LXX, the word occurs once, at Psalm 9:21. Its basic meaning is clear from its direct lexical definition, while the precise force it carries in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

This Greek Old Testament noun refers to a mountainous area or hill-country. It describes land marked by hills or mountains rather than flat ground. The word appears 11 times in the Greek Old Testament, in passages ranging from Numbers and Deuteronomy through Joshua, Jeremiah, 2 Chronicles, and Zechariah. Its precise reference—whether to a general mountainous region or a particular hill-country area—depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The basic idea remains terrain characterized by hills or mountains.

Opsiba, also rendered Opsiva, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 2 Kings 21:1. Because the available information identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding context, its specific referent cannot be explained further here. The name itself carries no broader lexical meaning beyond identifying the person or entity named in that passage.

This adjective means “all-holy,” describing someone or something wholly sacred and holy. It expresses complete holiness rather than a partial or limited degree of holiness. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, the word occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its appearances are recorded at 4 Maccabees 7:4 and 14:7. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain precisely what or whom it describes in each passage.

This word means “shoulder strap,” a noun for a band or fastening worn over the shoulder. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 28:14. The word therefore identifies a specific piece of clothing or equipment rather than expressing an action, quality, or person. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding description, but its basic meaning is clear: a strap associated with the shoulder.

This verb means “go all around,” describing movement through an area or among places rather than simply going to one point. It is used six times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, with most occurrences in Zechariah and one in 2 Samuel. The central idea remains movement around or throughout a place; the precise force in any particular verse depends on its surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “shepherd”: to act as a shepherd toward a flock. It describes shepherding as an action rather than naming the shepherd himself. The word occurs 52 times across 50 Old Testament verses in the Greek LXX, showing repeated use for shepherding language throughout that corpus. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and whether the wording is literal or figurative.

This word means “wool,” the soft fiber obtained from sheep. It is a noun naming a material, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times across six verses, especially in Judges 6, where wool is used in Gideon’s requests for a sign, and also in references connected with a sheep owner and human dependence from birth. Its basic meaning remains the material itself; the surrounding verse determines what is being said about it.

This noun means “great-grandfather,” referring to a male ancestor two generations above a person’s grandfather. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Exodus 10:6. The word identifies family ancestry rather than describing an action, emotion, or character trait. Its basic meaning is therefore straightforward: a father’s father’s father, or the corresponding ancestor through the family line. The surrounding verse supplies the specific family relationship intended there.
